# Core Programming Model

Covers Temporal's fundamental concepts: workflows, activities, message passing,
task queues, child workflows, continue-as-new, and execution limits.

## Workflows

A **Workflow Definition** is code written in a general-purpose language (Go,
Java, TypeScript, Python) that defines a sequence of steps [1]. A **Workflow
Type** maps to a definition, distinguishing one workflow kind from another [1].
A **Workflow Execution** is a running instance combining a definition with an
execution request [1].

Workflows progress through Commands and Events recorded in an **Event
History** [1]. This enables durability: "They can run—and keep running—for
years, even if the underlying infrastructure fails" [1]. The system
"automatically recreate[s] its pre-failure state so it can continue right
where it left off" [1].

**Deterministic Constraints**: "Workflows must follow deterministic constraints
to ensure consistent replay behavior" [1]. Operations that produce
non-deterministic results (system clock, random numbers, external I/O) must
be placed in activities, not workflow code.

## Activities

Activities are units of work that perform actual operations — API calls,
database writes, file processing [4]. Unlike workflows, activities are not
subject to determinism constraints [4]. Only input, output, and retry attempts
are tracked in Event History [4].

## Message Passing

Three message types enable communication with running workflows [2]:

| Type | Semantics | Event History | Worker Required |
|------|-----------|---------------|-----------------|
| **Queries** | Synchronous read-only | No entries | No (works on completed) |
| **Signals** | Async write, fire-and-forget | Never recorded | No |
| **Updates** | Sync write with response | Adds entries if accepted | Yes |

Queries: "read requests. They can read the current state of the Workflow but
cannot block" [2].

Signals: "asynchronous write requests. They cause changes in the running
Workflow, but you cannot await any response or error" [2].

Updates: "synchronous, tracked write requests. The sender of the Update can
wait for a response on completion or an error on failure" [2].

## Task Queues

A Task Queue is "a lightweight, dynamically allocated queue that one or more
Worker Entities poll for Tasks" [3]. Three types exist: Activity, Workflow,
and Nexus [3].

Key characteristics:
- No explicit registration required — created on demand [3]
- Workers use synchronous RPC polling, requesting tasks only "when it has
  spare capacity, avoiding overloading itself" [3]
- Workflow and Activity Tasks persist: "When a Worker Process goes down, the
  messages remain until the Worker recovers" [3]
- Nexus and Query Tasks are not persisted — they use "sync matching" [3]
- Default **4 partitions** per queue; single-partition is "almost always
  first-in, first-out" [3]
- Support "Task Routing" and "server-side throttling" [3]

## Child Workflows

Child Workflow Executions are spawned from within a parent Workflow in the
same Namespace [4]. Each child has its own Event History, enabling workload
partitioning (e.g., "1,000 Children × 1,000 Activities = 1M operations") [4].

| Aspect | Child Workflow | Activity |
|--------|----------------|----------|
| API Access | Full Workflow APIs, determinism required | No Workflow APIs, no constraints |
| Cancellation | Can survive parent (ABANDON policy) | Always canceled with parent |
| State Tracking | All changes in Event History | Only input/output/retries |

Default guidance: "When in doubt, use an Activity" [4].

Practical recommendation: parent should not spawn more than **~1,000** children
(each generates events in parent history) [4]. Hard limit is 2,000 pending
child executions [6].

"Child Workflows do not carry over when the Parent uses Continue-As-New" [4].
Communication only via asynchronous Signals — no shared local state [4].

## Continue-As-New

Continue-As-New checkpoints a Workflow's state and starts a fresh execution
with the same Workflow ID but a different Run ID [5]. The new execution gets
a fresh Event History, with state passed as arguments [5].

Use cases:
- **Event history management**: prevent hitting the 51,200 event / 50 MB
  limit [5][6]
- **Code freshness**: avoid running on stale code versions [5]

Workflows implementing repeated Continue-As-New represent "durable objects,
not just processes" — the **Entity Workflow Pattern** [5].

Temporal provides a "Continue-As-New Suggested" signal when approaching
performance limits [5]. The resulting chain of executions forms an "Execution
Chain" maintaining logical continuity [5].

## Execution Limits

| Limit | Value | Source |
|-------|-------|--------|
| Event History hard limit | 51,200 events OR 50 MB | [6] |
| Event History warning | 10,240 events OR 10 MB | [6] |
| Pending Activities | 2,000 (default, configurable) | [6] |
| Pending Child Workflows | 2,000 (default, configurable) | [6] |
| Pending Signals | 2,000 (default, configurable) | [6] |
| Pending Cancellation Requests | 2,000 (default, configurable) | [6] |
| Concurrent Nexus Operations | 30 (hard limit) | [6] |
| Task Queue partitions | 4 (default) | [3] |

When pending operation limits are reached, "the Workflow Task Execution will
fail and get retried" [6]. Limits are adjustable via dynamic configuration [6].

## Failure Type Hierarchy

All failures extend a base class: `TemporalFailure` (TS/Java/PHP) or
`FailureError` (Python) [7].

| Failure Type | Description |
|-------------|-------------|
| ApplicationFailure | "the only type of Temporal Failure created and thrown by user code" [7] |
| ActivityFailure | Wrapper with activity metadata; actual failure in `cause` field [7] |
| ChildWorkflowFailure | Wrapper for child workflow failures [7] |
| TimeoutFailure | Timeouts; includes "last Heartbeat details" [7] |
| CancelledFailure | Successful cancellation [7] |
| TerminatedFailure | Workflow termination [7] |

Critical distinction: in Workflows, non-Temporal exceptions cause **Workflow
Task retry** (unlimited, blocking the workflow) while ApplicationFailure errors
**fail the execution immediately** [7]. In Activities, non-Temporal errors
are auto-converted to ApplicationFailure with `non_retryable=false` [7].

Failures propagate via nested `cause` fields:
Workflow → ActivityFailure → ApplicationFailure/TimeoutFailure [7].

## Gaps and Limitations

- Temporal Cloud-specific limits may differ from self-hosted defaults [6]
- The `MaxCallbacksPerWorkflow` limit value is not disclosed in documentation [6]
- Nexus Task Queue type and its use cases are not fully documented in the
  fetched sources
